posts.title: The Herdsman From Tamale
posts.excerpt: This one isn't from Accra. I was in Tamale for a wedding and stepped out when I got the chance. Someone mentioned there was a herd nearby.
posts.body:
This one isn't from Accra. I was in Tamale for a wedding and stepped out when I got the chance. Someone mentioned there was a herd nearby and I wanted to see it. I found it. And behind it was this guy.

I reached for my phone the second I saw him. I just knew: if I didn't take the shot right then, that was it. Gone.

He noticed the phone as soon as it came out. He was friendly but a little shy, and he just kept moving. He was genuinely trying to catch up to the herd, which had already moved ahead without him. He kept smiling the whole time though. I followed, he kept going, I kept shooting.

I only noticed the moon when I went back through the photos later. It's sitting faintly in the far distance behind him. I wasn't looking for it at all. I was completely locked on him. I looked at the image again and was so glad it made the frame. There's no way I would've planned that.

He was clearly in a hurry. The herd was pulling further ahead. I thought we were done.

Then right at the last bit, he turned around. Stood still for a few seconds. Posed. Smiled at me properly. Waved. Then turned back and disappeared into the greens after a herd I could no longer see.

This photograph is from just before that. Before he turned around.

Tamale, June 2023. One of the most intriguing moments of my photography journey.

posts.title: Why I Shoot With My Phone
posts.excerpt: There's a theory that constraints breed creativity. I've been testing it for four years with nothing but the camera in my pocket.
posts.body:
There's a theory that constraints breed creativity. I've been testing it for four years with nothing but the camera in my pocket.

When I started photographing seriously, I had a DSLR. It was a good camera — technically capable, undeniably impressive. But I noticed something: people saw it coming. The moment I raised it, expressions changed. The street shifted. The light on a woman's face at Makola market would flatten the instant she noticed the lens.

The phone changed everything. It's invisible. People look at their own phones all day; one more person staring at a small rectangle is unremarkable. It gave me access to moments that the DSLR kept locked behind a wall of self-consciousness.

The technical limitations forced me to think harder about light. You can't zoom your way to a good photograph on a phone — you have to move, get closer, wait. The discipline became part of the practice.

posts.title: On Editions and Why They Matter
posts.excerpt: Limiting editions is a promise. Here's what that promise actually means.
posts.body:
Limiting editions is a promise. Here's what that promise actually means.

When I say a print is an edition of 15, I mean exactly 15 will ever be produced — signed, numbered, certified. Not 15 this year, not 15 and then a reprint. 15. When they're gone, that's it.

This matters for two reasons. The first is artistic: scarcity forces a kind of accountability. If I commit to only 15 of something, I have to be sure that something deserves to exist in the world. It can't be a filler piece. The discipline sharpens the edit.

The second reason is for collectors. When you buy a print, you're not buying a JPEG someone else can reproduce infinitely. You're buying a specific, numbered object; physical proof of a moment, certified by my signature and a document that travels with it. The certificate isn't bureaucracy; it's a record of what you own and why it's real.
